processing: Ripe pu-erh combined with rose blossoms and pressed, often as a small cake or tuo; the proportion and the method differ by maker.
harvest_season: No defined tea season; sold by pressing year, like other ripe pu-erh blends.
appearance_dry: Dark brown pressed leaf flecked with dried rose petals or buds.
appearance_liquor: Deep red-brown and clear, sometimes a little warmer in tone than plain shu.
appearance_wet: Soft dark leaf with faded, limp petals through it.
taste_profile: A clean, sweet ripe base with rose perfume; one maker's version is described with a distinct cinnamon note. Expect low bitterness.

brewing.notes: Rinse briefly. Keep steeps short at first; long steeps turn rose petals slightly bitter and flatten the perfume.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year in small cakes (100 g is one format) and tuos. The ripe base can keep improving, but rose aroma tends to fade, so a few years is the sensible window. A year on the label is not a promise of age value here.
description:
Rose and ripe pu-erh are an old friend of southern Chinese tea snacks and drink stalls, and this tea presses the combination into a cake or tuo. Meigui hua just means rose blossom, so the name tells you the ingredient, not the origin of any one recipe.

The tea starts as ordinary wet-piled shu, usually from Yunnan big-leaf material, with the rose joined to it before pressing. There is no single standard for how, or for how much rose goes in, so these teas range from a light floral lift to a full-on perfume.

In the cup the rose softens the earthy edge of the shu, leaving something sweet and rounded. Some versions pick up a warm, cinnamon-like spice. Use short steeps and pour fully, because petals left to stew turn dull.

Look for visible petals and a natural smell, and be wary of very strong perfume. If you like this, compare it with a plain ripe tea from the same maker to see what the rose is really adding.
history: Little is documented about who first pressed rose with ripe pu-erh. The pairing itself is described as a traditional one in southern tea snacks and drinks. Today's pressed forms come from various makers, such as the small Xingyang Workshop series of 2017 based on herbs, fruit and flowers.
